claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 within ±5% of experimental values.
The surrogate can reduce computational time by at least 5× relative to full-resolution simulations.
Representing lamellar thickness and grain-boundary orientation statistics enables the surrogate to capture dominant load-transfer and crack-deflection mechanisms.
The HfNbTiVAl10 alloy is fabricated by directional solidification.
The alloy is annealed at 1200 °C for 2 h.
The resulting microstructure contains alternating coarse-grained regions of approximately 10 µm and fine-lamellar regions of approximately 1 µm.
The surrogate will be trained on a sparse set of crystal-plasticity FEM and cohesive-zone fracture simulations augmented by measured microstructural descriptors.
Lamellar thickness distribution, grain-boundary misorientation distribution, and the fine-to-coarse region volume-fraction ratio are predictive structural mediators.
Enforcing elastic constitutive laws, crystal-slip kinetics, and fracture-cohesion laws allows the surrogate to learn effective stiffness, yield onset, and crack growth.
Load transfer across heterointerfaces governs the predicted mechanical response.
Crack deflection at lamellar boundaries governs fracture-related behavior.
Young’s modulus will be approximately 100 GPa and predicted within ±2 GPa.
Yield strength will be approximately 700 MPa and predicted within ±20 MPa.
Fracture toughness will be approximately 15 MPa√m and predicted within ±0.2 MPa√m.
Surrogate inference will require less than 1 h on a single GPU.
Full-resolution crystal-plasticity FEM requires approximately 5 GPU-hours per case.
Full-resolution crystal-plasticity FEM exhibits errors of up to ±10% relative to experiments.
Model accuracy may degrade when lamellar thickness lies outside 0.5–2 µm.
Model accuracy may degrade for compositions differing by more than 5 at% from HfNbTiVAl10.
Limited high-strain training data and unmodeled phenomena such as dynamic recrystallization could increase prediction errors.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires predictions within ±5%, and the property-specific outcome tolerances are even tighter, but the predeclared falsification rule only rejects property errors greater than ±10%. Thus, errors between the stated tolerance and 10% would violate the hypothesis without triggering its falsification rule.
